title: The Architecture of Agency: Maya and the Employees Nobody Hired
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Through a narrative case study about a fictional executive named Maya, whose company simultaneously sends a strategically important customer a payment warning, an upsell pitch, a service credit, and an adoption-concern message -- each generated by a different AI agent acting entirely reasonably within its own domain -- Richard Claydon argues that the deepest risk of enterprise AI adoption is organisational rather than technical. Each of the five agents involved (Sales, Customer Success, Finance, Service, Deal Desk) had a sound business case, measurable benefits, and formal approval, yet their combined, uncoordinated action produced an incoherent and damaging customer experience that no single function could see or own. Claydon introduces "shadow agency" as an extension of shadow IT -- action an organisation does not fully know it has authorised, as opposed to technology it does not know it has -- and argues that AI removes the everyday human friction (comparing notes, checking with colleagues) that used to catch these contradictions before they reached customers. The piece closes by arguing that accountability has not kept pace with distributed agency: the account executive remained formally responsible for the customer despite never approving any of the individual actions, and organisations must design who can act, who can see combined action across agents, who can stop it, and who carries the consequence -- or by default, "the nearest responsible human" will absorb a role nobody designed.
points: Each of five AI agents (Sales, Customer Success, Finance, Service, Deal Desk) acted reasonably and defensibly within its own local business case, yet their uncoordinated combined action produced contradictory, damaging messages to the same strategic customer within a single afternoon.

Claydon coins "shadow agency" as the AI-era counterpart to shadow IT: shadow IT is technology an organisation doesn't know it has, while shadow agency is action an organisation doesn't fully know it has authorised.

AI removes friction inside individual processes (faster collections, faster triage, faster expansion detection) while simultaneously accelerating collisions between those processes, because the human friction that used to catch contradictions -- comparing notes, checking with colleagues -- disappears along with the delay.

Accountability has not moved at the same pace as agency: the account executive remained formally responsible for the customer relationship despite never approving any of the four individual agent actions that caused the incident.

The piece argues a serious AI business case must account for the organisational costs AI creates around itself -- who supervises agents, resolves contradictions, and reconstructs events -- not just the efficiency gains each individual agent produces.
quotes: The company had now managed to tell that customer, almost simultaneously, that it owed them money, should buy more from them, deserved compensation because their service had failed, and was not using enough of what it had already bought.

Maya sent a message back. Who approved all of this? The reply came almost immediately. That's the problem. Nobody did. She would later discover that this was slightly misleading. Several things had approved it. That was worse.
Organisations are fairly good at rejecting obviously bad ideas. Individually attractive ideas that combine into something nobody intended are considerably more troublesome.

The company had built several systems capable of forming locally sensible interpretations of the same customer. Those systems had no shared interpretation of the customer as a whole. The customer was where the organisation finally came back together. What came back together looked absurd.
Shadow IT is technology the organisation does not fully know it has. Shadow agency is action the organisation does not fully know it has authorised. The consequences travel further.
The AI business case is incomplete until it accounts for the organisation AI creates around itself.

AI could make the organisation dramatically more productive. It could also create a new organisational role before anyone thought to design it: the person expected to reconstruct what distributed intelligence had done, reconcile competing consequences, explain the result, repair the relationships and remain accountable for the whole.
